name: AI Executive Readiness — The Enterprise Scorecard
subtitle: The AI Executive Readiness Scorecard
rule_text: each scope is scored separately; level = band of the scope overall mean of 12 ratings; floor = lowest dimension, reported; difference = self minus leadership

scopes.label: Your organization’s leaders
scopes.group_label: Respondents’ assessments of the organization’s leaders

text.instructions: Answer each question twice. First, rate yourself and then rate your organization’s leaders collectively. Base your ratings on current practices and experience.
text.comparison_note: The difference is your score minus your rating of the organization’s leaders. A positive value means you rated yourself higher. A negative value means you rated the leaders higher. Equal scores can both be low or both be high. These differences describe your perceptions, not demonstrated performance.
text.disclaimer: This scorecard is a self-assessment. Scores describe the respondent’s stated practices and perceptions of the organization’s leaders. They do not constitute an audit, legal advice, or professional advice.

rungs.name: Undeveloped
rungs.description: The assessed practices have yet to be developed.

rungs.name: Emerging
rungs.description: Some practices are present, but their use is limited.

rungs.name: Developing
rungs.description: The practices are developing but are not yet consistent.

rungs.name: Established
rungs.description: The practices are generally reliable, with some gaps.

rungs.name: Embedded
rungs.description: The practices are consistently demonstrated and reviewed.

dimensions.name: Direction and judgment
dimensions.description: Leaders need to explain which business problems AI should help solve. They also need to judge whether an AI recommendation fits the situation and decide when ethical concerns require them to reject a proposal.
dimensions.summary_line: Identify the problems AI should help solve and exercise judgment about its use.

guide.what: Leaders provide direction by identifying the specific business problems AI should help solve, rather than by reaching to find a use for the newest technological breakthroughs. Good judgment involves knowing whether you can trust the advice an AI system provides and whether its recommendation will survive contact with real humans in the external world. Your leadership team also needs to decide which uses of AI it would reject on ethical grounds, even when those uses offer financial benefits.
guide.why: AI systems influence what leaders notice, which options they consider, and what they regard as a good outcome. The people who develop and configure those systems make choices about what information matters and which objectives take priority. Those choices may conflict with the organization’s own priorities and ethical principles. If leaders accept those choices without questioning them, AI can shape the direction of the business without a deliberate leadership decision. Leaders need to preserve their ability to form independent judgments about the advice they receive.
guide.how: Take one proposed AI initiative and write down the business problem it is meant to solve. Examine a recommendation the system might make, then ask the people affected what following it would mean in practice. Discuss what evidence would persuade you to accept the recommendation and what consequences would lead you to reject it.

items.label: Business problems
items.question: How clearly can you / your organization’s leaders explain which business problems AI should help solve?

self.low: You struggle to name a specific business problem that AI should help solve or explain why it deserves attention.
self.high: You can name specific business problems that AI should help solve, explain why they matter, and describe what a useful improvement would look like.

leadership.low: Leaders struggle to name specific business problems that AI should help solve or give conflicting accounts of why those problems deserve attention.
leadership.high: Leaders can name specific business problems that AI should help solve, explain why they matter, and describe what useful improvements would look like.

items.label: Judgment in context
items.question: How well can you / your organization’s leaders recognize when an AI recommendation is wrong for the situation, even if its facts are correct?

self.low: You generally accept an AI recommendation once its facts and calculations appear correct. You rarely examine what following it would mean in the actual situation.
self.high: You examine the consequences of following an AI recommendation. You can identify circumstances or human needs that it overlooks and explain when a different decision is needed.

leadership.low: Leaders generally accept AI recommendations once their facts and calculations appear correct. They rarely examine what following them would mean in the actual situation.
leadership.high: Leaders examine the consequences of following AI recommendations. They can identify circumstances or human needs that the recommendations overlook and explain when different decisions are needed.

items.label: Ethical commitment
items.question: How prepared are you / your organization’s leaders to reject an AI proposal on ethical grounds, even if it would save money?

self.low: You have not established which ethical concerns would lead you to reject an AI proposal. Expected savings tend to settle the decision.
self.high: You can explain which ethical concerns would lead you to reject an AI proposal. You can show, through a decision or a realistic case, how you would uphold those limits despite the savings offered.

leadership.low: Leaders have not established which ethical concerns would lead them to reject an AI proposal. Expected savings tend to settle the decision.
leadership.high: Leaders can explain which ethical concerns would lead them to reject an AI proposal. They can show, through decisions or realistic cases, how they would uphold those limits despite the savings offered.

dimensions.name: AI fluency
dimensions.description: AI fluency combines practical experience with an understanding of what AI can and cannot do. Leaders need to check AI outputs and assess the likely benefits, costs, and risks of proposals to use it.
dimensions.summary_line: Understand AI through practical use, check its outputs, and assess proposals.

guide.what: AI fluency is the practical understanding that lets leaders judge what an AI system can contribute to their work. For example, an AI assistant may produce a clear briefing while inventing a source or leaving out a fact that changes the conclusion. A fluent leader understands what the assistant has contributed and what still needs to be checked by someone who knows the subject.
guide.why: A polished demonstration can hide the work needed to make an AI system useful. The value of its outputs may depend on clean data, carefully chosen examples, or extensive human review. Leaders who cannot identify those conditions may overestimate the benefits and underestimate the cost of using the system in their own organization.
guide.how: Use an AI system on a task you know well enough to assess independently. Compare its output with your own analysis and investigate any differences. Record where it saved time, where it introduced errors, and how much checking it required. Discuss those findings with other leaders before deciding whether the same approach would be useful in other parts of the organization.

items.label: Understanding through use
items.question: Based on practical experience, how well can you / your organization’s leaders explain what AI can and cannot do?

self.low: You rely mainly on descriptions or demonstrations of AI. You have little direct experience of using it on tasks that are relevant to your responsibilities.
self.high: You have used AI on tasks that are relevant to your responsibilities. You can explain what worked, what failed, and why its performance limits matter for those tasks.

leadership.low: Leaders rely mainly on descriptions or demonstrations of AI. They have little direct experience of using it on tasks that are relevant to their responsibilities.
leadership.high: Leaders have used AI on tasks that are relevant to their responsibilities. They can explain what worked, what failed, and why its performance limits matter for those tasks.

items.label: Checking AI outputs
items.question: How effectively can you / your organization’s leaders recognize and investigate errors in AI outputs before relying on them?

self.low: You tend to accept AI outputs when they sound plausible. You rarely check their sources, calculations, or important omissions.
self.high: You check important AI outputs against reliable sources or independent analysis. When you suspect an error, you investigate it or obtain qualified help before relying on the output.

leadership.low: Leaders tend to accept AI outputs when they sound plausible. They rarely check their sources, calculations, or important omissions.
leadership.high: Leaders check important AI outputs against reliable sources or independent analysis. When they suspect an error, they investigate it or obtain qualified help before relying on the output.

items.label: Assessing proposals
items.question: How well can you / your organization’s leaders assess the likely benefits, costs, and risks of an AI proposal?

self.low: You find it difficult to question the benefits claimed for an AI proposal or identify its continuing costs and significant risks.
self.high: You test the benefits claimed for an AI proposal against evidence. You examine implementation and continuing costs, significant risks, and what would make the investment worthwhile.

leadership.low: Leaders find it difficult to question the benefits claimed for AI proposals or identify their continuing costs and significant risks.
leadership.high: Leaders test the benefits claimed for AI proposals against evidence. They examine implementation and continuing costs, significant risks, and what would make each investment worthwhile.

dimensions.name: Leadership structure
dimensions.description: Leaders need clear responsibilities for AI-related changes and a way to coordinate decisions across departments. They also need to decide which work can be delegated to AI and give middle managers the knowledge and authority to shape its use.
dimensions.summary_line: Coordinate decisions and give people clear responsibilities and authority.

guide.what: Successful AI implementation depends on a leadership structure that assigns responsibilities and authority to meet the demands of working with AI. This means defining the roles of the board, senior executives, and middle managers, including how they make decisions together and which decisions each can make independently. A chief AI officer or a chief innovation and transformation officer can play a central role in this structure, but other leaders still need clearly defined responsibilities. Leaders also need to review those responsibilities as AI takes on tasks and decisions that people previously handled.
guide.why: AI affects decisions about investment, staffing, risk, and the services that an organization provides. A technology leader may understand the systems but lack the authority to make decisions in critical areas. If the rest of the leadership team treats AI as someone else’s responsibility, important decisions can be left unresolved or made without the right people involved. The organization may also delegate work to AI without deciding which responsibilities its managers should retain.
guide.how: Map the responsibilities that the board, senior executives, and middle managers have for AI. Identify which decisions each leader can make and which require leaders from different departments to decide together. Agree how those leaders will coordinate their work and resolve disagreements about priorities or resources. Involve middle managers in deciding which parts of their work can be delegated to AI and which require their own judgment. Give them the knowledge and authority that they need to carry out the responsibilities that remain with them.

items.label: Coordination across departments
items.question: How effectively do you / your organization’s leaders coordinate AI-related changes across departments?

self.low: You mainly address AI-related changes within your own area. Responsibilities or decisions that involve other departments often remain unresolved.
self.high: You work with the leaders of affected departments to assign responsibilities and resolve shared decisions. You follow through on your commitments and seek decisions from others when needed.

leadership.low: Leaders mainly address AI-related changes within their own departments. Responsibilities or decisions that involve several departments often remain unresolved.
leadership.high: Leaders assign responsibilities for AI-related changes, resolve decisions across departments, and follow through on shared commitments. People know who can resolve outstanding issues.

items.label: Delegating work to AI
items.question: How clearly have you / your organization’s leaders established which tasks and decisions can be delegated to AI and which must remain with people?

self.low: You have not made clear which tasks and decisions people in your area may delegate to AI or which require human judgment and approval.
self.high: You have made clear which tasks and decisions people in your area may delegate to AI. People understand what requires human judgment or approval and whom to ask when the boundary is uncertain.

leadership.low: Leaders have not made clear which tasks and decisions may be delegated to AI or which require human judgment and approval.
leadership.high: Leaders have made clear which tasks and decisions may be delegated to AI. People understand what requires human judgment or approval and whom to ask when the boundary is uncertain.

items.label: Middle managers’ influence
items.question: How effectively do you / your organization’s leaders enable middle managers to shape AI use in the work they oversee?

self.low: You give middle managers little influence over AI use in the work they oversee. They lack the knowledge, authority, or access to you that they need to get problems addressed.
self.high: You help middle managers gain the knowledge to design and test AI use in their teams’ work. You give them authority to make changes within their responsibilities and a reliable way to obtain decisions that require your approval.

leadership.low: Leaders give middle managers little influence over AI use in the work they oversee. Managers lack the knowledge, authority, or access to senior leaders that they need to get problems addressed.
leadership.high: Leaders help middle managers gain the knowledge to design and test AI use in their teams’ work. They give managers authority to make changes within their responsibilities and a reliable way to obtain decisions that require senior approval.

dimensions.name: Change and development
dimensions.description: Leaders need to help employees adapt when AI changes their jobs. They also need to respond constructively when people raise concerns or admit mistakes, and address gaps in their own ability to lead AI-related change.
dimensions.summary_line: Help people adapt, welcome questions, and develop your own leadership abilities.

guide.what: Leading AI-related change means helping people work through changes whose effects may not yet be clear. An AI tool can change employees’ responsibilities and leave them unsure whether their expertise still matters. Leaders need to understand those effects through continuing conversations with employees and be willing to revise their own approach as they learn.
guide.why: AI can change both the work that employees do and the demands that are placed on the people who lead them. Experience with earlier ways of working may not prepare leaders to guide those changes. Without effective leadership, employees may receive new responsibilities without the support to fulfill them, and difficulties can persist because people hesitate to raise them. Leaders need to learn from what happens in practice and develop their own abilities if they are to help others adapt.
guide.how: Ask employees to describe a difficulty they encountered when AI changed their work. Listen to what happened before proposing a solution, and agree what support you will provide. Return to find out whether that support helped. Ask what you could have handled better, then choose a leadership skill to develop and review your progress with a colleague.

items.label: Helping employees adapt
items.question: How well can you / your organization’s leaders help employees adapt when AI changes their jobs?

self.low: You mainly announce changes and expect employees to adapt. You struggle to address concerns about how roles will change or what people will need to learn.
self.high: You can demonstrate how you have helped employees work through changes in their roles. You explain what is changing, address concerns directly, and follow through when people encounter difficulties.

leadership.low: Leaders mainly announce changes and expect employees to adapt. They struggle to address concerns about how roles will change or what people will need to learn.
leadership.high: Leaders can demonstrate how they have helped employees work through changes in their roles. They explain what is changing, address concerns directly, and follow through when people encounter difficulties.

items.label: Responding to questions and mistakes
items.question: How safe is it for people to question an AI initiative or admit a mistake to you / your organization’s leadership team?

self.low: People have reason to expect blame or a defensive response when they question an AI initiative or admit a mistake to you.
self.high: People can question an AI initiative or admit a mistake to you without fearing unfair consequences. You listen, investigate concerns, and show how you have acted on what people tell you.

leadership.low: People have reason to expect blame or a defensive response when they question an AI initiative or admit a mistake to the leadership team.
leadership.high: People can question an AI initiative or admit a mistake to the leadership team without fearing unfair consequences. Leaders listen, investigate concerns, and show how they have acted on what people tell them.

items.label: Developing leadership abilities
items.question: How systematically do you / your organization’s leaders identify and address gaps in your / their own ability to lead AI-related change?

self.low: You rarely seek feedback on your ability to lead AI-related change. Any learning is occasional and has no clear development goal.
self.high: You seek feedback and identify specific gaps in your ability to lead AI-related change. You set development goals, practice the relevant skills, and review evidence of progress.

leadership.low: Leaders rarely seek feedback on their ability to lead AI-related change. Any learning is occasional and has no clear development goals.
leadership.high: Leaders seek feedback and identify specific gaps in their ability to lead AI-related change. They set development goals, practice the relevant skills, and review evidence of progress.

correlation_metrics.label: Executive meetings with AI as a decision item

established.note: Strong practices across the four dimensions.

developing.note: Practices are developing with some inconsistency.

fluent.note: Practical AI understanding is ahead of coordination and employee support.

coordinated.note: Clear leadership responsibilities with less practical AI experience.

supportive.note: Strong support for people with less practical AI experience.

starting.note: Most assessed practices have yet to develop.
